# Directions: Editorial Family

Type-led directions where hierarchy, rhythm, and reading carry the experience. Precedent IDs refer
to the Experience Skills observation log (observed 2026-09-24).

---

## Editorial

**Philosophy:** the reader's attention is the product; typography, measure, and rhythm do the work
that containers do elsewhere.

| Aspect | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Suits | Publishing, long-form, documentation hubs, research, considered commerce, annual reports |
| Unsuitable | High-frequency tools, dense data operations, games |
| Composition | Reading column with purposeful margins; headline–deck–body; pull quotes; image inside the text flow |
| Typography | A serif or characterful display for headlines, a comfortable text face at 16–20 px, 45–80 characters per line |
| Surface & shape | Flat paper-like surfaces, hairline rules, few containers |
| Imagery | Art-directed photography or diagrams with captions; images serve the story |
| Palette | Warm editorial or restrained neutral; one accent tied to sections or links |
| Motion | Almost none; gentle reveals only in storytelling pieces |
| Interaction | Standard links and navigation; table of contents for long pieces |
| Accessibility | Measure, line height, and link visibility matter most; do not use light grey body text |

**Fails when:** prose is broken into cards; measure stretches to full width; the display face lacks a
companion for the site's other scripts. **Slop risk:** "editorial" as a label for a centered serif
headline on an otherwise generic page. **Precedent:** The Guardian (GU3, GU4), Wikipedia (WPd1),
Our World in Data (OW1, OW2), Aesop (AE1). **Adapt, don't copy:** take the reading structure, not a
newspaper's masthead.

## Expressive editorial

**Philosophy:** editorial structure with deliberate drama: scale contrast, art direction, layouts
that change per story.

| Aspect | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Suits | Culture magazines, brand storytelling, data journalism, campaign microsites |
| Unsuitable | Repeated tasks; anything users do daily |
| Composition | Editorial spreads, asymmetric splits, full-bleed breaks, stat-led openings |
| Typography | Large display type used as image; mixed weights; occasional hand-lettering |
| Surface & shape | Varies per piece; coherent within a piece |
| Imagery | Commissioned illustration, bespoke charts, story-specific color |
| Palette | Per-story palettes inside a stable brand frame |
| Motion | Scroll-linked storytelling with a reduced-motion equivalent |
| Interaction | Standard navigation around bespoke story interactions |
| Accessibility | Bespoke charts need text alternatives; scroll storytelling needs a non-scroll path |

**Fails when:** every page is a spectacle, including navigation and search. **Slop risk:** random
scale changes without a story reason. **Precedent:** The Pudding (PU1–PU3), Patagonia campaign (PA1).
**Adapt:** keep the index stable; let each story vary.

## Fashion editorial

**Philosophy:** image and type as spectacle; extreme contrast and cropping; the brand is attitude.

| Aspect | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Suits | Fashion, luxury campaigns, photographers, events |
| Unsuitable | Utilities, public service, finance, anything requiring trust through clarity |
| Composition | Full-bleed image, poster-like type, sparse annotation |
| Typography | High-contrast Didone or extreme condensed sans; very large sizes |
| Surface & shape | Flat; image does the work |
| Imagery | Commissioned photography; unconventional crops |
| Palette | Monochrome with one signature color, or image-derived |
| Motion | Slow cross-fades, cinematic cuts |
| Interaction | Minimal chrome; must still expose price and size quickly on commerce pages |
| Accessibility | Text on images needs scrims; tiny annotation type often fails contrast |

**Fails when:** it hides the buy path or product facts. **Slop risk:** high-contrast serif and big
whitespace as "premium" with stock photography. **Precedent:** Nike campaign hero (NK1) as a
commerce-compatible adaptation. **Adapt:** spectacle above, efficient commerce structure beneath.

## Text-first

**Philosophy:** the fastest possible path to words and links; almost no visual system beyond type.

| Aspect | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Suits | Reference, forums, link aggregators, personal writing, changelogs |
| Unsuitable | Visual discovery, brand-led consumer products, games |
| Composition | Single column or list; numbered items; minimal chrome |
| Typography | System or one text face; hierarchy by weight and color |
| Surface & shape | None |
| Imagery | None or rare |
| Palette | One accent (often the only color on the page) |
| Motion | None |
| Interaction | Links; keyboard-friendly; very fast |
| Accessibility | Watch small targets and low-contrast metadata |

**Fails when:** used for newcomers or touch-first audiences without larger targets. **Precedent:**
Hacker News (HN1, HN2), Wikipedia mobile (WPm1); Are.na (ARN1–ARN3) shows the register at its most
extreme: no imagery, no cards, one button, identity carried entirely by a small glyph mark and a
distinctive writing voice — including a self-description written as an open, literally editable
outline (ARN1) and a live-computed running duration standing in for a static founding date (ARN2).
**Adapt:** ARN2's move — replacing a static fact with a small piece of real, live-computed data — is
a cheap way to make plain text feel considered rather than templated, without adding any visual
system at all; keep the speed; raise contrast and target size.

## Archival

**Philosophy:** everything is catalogued, dated, versioned, and citable.

| Aspect | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Suits | Museums, research, records, datasets, knowledge bases |
| Unsuitable | Fast consumer flows |
| Composition | Index-first lists, detail pages with metadata panels |
| Typography | Serif for content, mono or small caps for metadata |
| Surface & shape | Paper tones, rules, catalog cards |
| Imagery | Documentary photography with captions and provenance |
| Palette | Warm neutrals, muted accents |
| Motion | None |
| Interaction | Search, filters, citation tools, version history |
| Accessibility | Dense metadata must remain readable at 200% zoom |

**Fails when:** metadata overwhelms the item. **Precedent:** Our World in Data "Cite this article",
"Browse past versions" (OW2); Wikipedia revision notice (WPm1); Google Arts & Culture (GAC1–GAC3)
offers geographic browsing ("Nearby") as a first-class peer to topical browsing rather than a buried
filter (GAC1), with map controls following ordinary convention (GAC2) and depth in featured content
suggested through a simple stacked-card offset rather than heavy rendering (GAC3). **Adapt:**
credibility tools beside the content; for a real-world/museum archive specifically, offering location
as an equally-weighted browse dimension (not just topic or date) helps when the underlying items are
tied to physical places.
